analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Drugs is a generic API manufacturer that rode the COVID-era China+1 tailwind to peak earnings in 2021 (₹280 Cr PAT) but has since structurally declined — revenue fell from ₹2,716 Cr (2023) to ₹2,387 Cr (2025) and operating margin compressed to a thin 6.16%. The business fails my core financial thresholds on debt, ROE, margins, and FCF yield simultaneously.
key_strengths: Established API franchise since 1984 with a diversified product portfolio across anti-infectives, NSAIDs, and antidiabetics — real and defensible
Promoter holding stable at 55.03% — no stake reduction, which is the minimum I expect
OCF positive all 5 consecutive years (₹245 Cr in FY25), demonstrating the business can at least generate cash from operations
key_risks: Revenue and profitability in structural decline since FY22 peak — PAT down 40% from ₹280 Cr (FY21) to ₹168 Cr (FY25), EBITDA CAGR only 3.9% over 9 years
Debt/Equity at 0.39 exceeds my hard limit of 0.3, and total debt rose to ₹615 Cr while cash stands at a negligible ₹5 Cr — very thin buffer
Heavy capex cycle (₹177–226 Cr/year) generating near-zero FCF (₹67 Cr in FY25); FCF yield of ~2% is less than half my 5% minimum — capital is being consumed, not generated
red_flags: Operating margin at 6.16% is borderline commodity-level — well below my 8% floor; this signals weak pricing power in generic APIs
Finance costs expanding (₹24 Cr FY22 → ₹39 Cr FY25) while earnings contract — classic sign of a business borrowing to stay afloat
ROE of only 12.7% and ROCE of 13.1% are below my 15% threshold — the business is not earning adequate returns on the capital being deployed
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aarti Drugs is a textbook case of a cyclical business mistaken for a compounder. The FY21 earnings spike (PAT ₹280 Cr, EBITDA ₹490 Cr) was a COVID-era windfall from API supply disruptions and China+1 sentiment — not a structural re-rating. By FY25, PAT has fallen back to ₹168 Cr, revenue has contracted two consecutive years, and EBITDA has nearly halved. What concerns me most is the 6.16% operating margin — this is not what I see in quality healthcare businesses; it is what I see in low-value intermediates with no pricing power. I built DMart on the principle that sustainable margins, even if modest, must be consistent. Here they are neither.

The balance sheet also troubles me. Debt of ₹615 Cr against virtually no cash (₹5 Cr) with an active capex programme of ₹177 Cr/year means the company is running lean on safety margin. CWIP at ₹179 Cr suggests the capacity build is not yet complete, so capex pressure will continue before returns materialise. Debt/Equity of 0.39 already breaches my threshold, and if earnings remain under pressure, this will worsen. At a P/E of 16.8x, the market is not pricing this as distressed — but the fundamentals reflect a business under meaningful stress. I need consistency, clean balance sheets, and returns above cost of capital. Aarti Drugs currently offers none of the three.
